medical.title: Research highlights long-term health risks of gestational diabetes
medical.summary: Gestational diabetes is often viewed as a complication of pregnancy that resolves after delivery, but a new review led by researchers from LSU's Pennington Biomedical Research Center shows that its health implications can extend for years, increasing cardiometabolic risks for mothers and potentially affecting the future health of their children.

medical.title: ICE operation in Minneapolis likely led to fewer health care visits for Spanish-speaking patients, analysis finds
medical.summary: From December 2025 through February 2026, about 2,000 US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents descended on the Minneapolis-Saint Paul metro area, which increased raids, arrests, and violence as part of Operation Metro Surge (OMS).

medical.title: Music before and during coronary angiography linked to lower blood pressure
medical.summary: Music therapy before and during an often stressful procedure to visualize blood flow to coronary arteries (coronary angiography) is associated with lower systolic blood pressure—the higher number in a reading—according to the results of a comparative clinical trial published online in the journal Heart.

medical.title: From primal instinct to persistent preoccupation: Measuring 'food noise'
medical.summary: How people think about food continues to evolve. For early hunter-gatherers, food meant survival. Thoughts about food focused mainly on where to find it. As people learned to farm, thoughts about food shifted from something hunted or caught to something cultivated.

medical.title: Parents strongly accept intestinal ultrasound for pediatric IBD monitoring
medical.summary: Parents of children with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) report strong acceptance of intestinal ultrasound (IUS) for disease monitoring, according to a study published online Nov. 17 in JPGN Reports.

medical.title: Could blowing your nose make cold symptoms worse?
medical.summary: Few things are more frustrating than dealing with a runny nose when you're sick. No matter how many times you blow your nose, a few minutes later it's full of snot again and the sniffles are back.

medical.title: Many languages, one common neural code
'I'm amazed every day': Woman marks one year with a pig kidney
medical.summary: A New Hampshire woman has now lived for one year with a kidney from a gene-edited pig, the longest any patient is known to have done so.

medical.title: Significant decrease in Black-white mortality gap during past 30 years
medical.summary: A major health gap in America is shrinking. A new study by researchers at the American Cancer Society (ACS) shows the historic divide in death rates between Black and white men and women in the United States narrowed dramatically between 1993 and 2023. Excess mortality among Black adults plummeted by 56% for men and 68% for women.

medical.title: AI can predict antidepressant response, but does not understand all patients equally
medical.summary: George Mason University researchers have revealed just how much health literacy can influence AI's ability to understand patients. In a new study involving simulated patients, an AI antidepressant decision aid correctly identified medical information 82% of the time when patients used precise medical language, but less than half the time when they described their health in vaguer or more informal terms.

medical.title: When antidepressants don't help, could ketamine be an option?
medical.summary: Once known mainly as a surgical anesthetic, ketamine is now an option for people whose depression hasn't eased with standard medications and therapy.

medical.title: How the brain's visual system shapes lasting fear memories
medical.summary: Researchers at McGovern Medical School at UTHealth Houston have discovered how the brain's visual system plays an active role in transforming threatening experiences into lasting fear memories and how noninvasive brain stimulation can interrupt this process.

medical.title: Not just a phase: Measuring the long-term toll of high school substance use
medical.summary: High schoolers who smoke cigarettes, use cannabis or take other drugs face a higher risk of dying earlier in adulthood, according to a five-decade University of Michigan study.

medical.title: New Year's resolutions: Starting small today could work better than waiting until January
medical.summary: Every year, millions of people promise to start the new year by losing weight, eating better and exercising more. January feels like a natural moment for a fresh start. But big resolutions create a lot of pressure and are hard to keep up.

medical.title: Lack of data hinders genetic screening for heart failure in the Brazilian population
medical.summary: The low representation of Brazilians in global genomic databases compromises the accuracy of tests used to investigate the causes of heart failure. This is according to a study by the University of São Paulo (USP), which revealed an additional limitation of these tests: interpreting results is significantly more difficult when analyzing DNA segments of African or Indigenous ancestry.

medical.title: How sensory neurons help the brain pursue its goals
medical.summary: A new Yale study offers insight into a fundamental question in neuroscience: How does the nervous system transform sensory information into signals that help us achieve our goals?

medical.title: One in 12 children with Lyme disease show signs of Powassan virus co-infection
medical.summary: The prevalence of Powassan virus infection in U.S. children with suspected Lyme disease is higher than previously thought, according to a new study published in Clinical Infectious Diseases.

medical.title: Only 13% of lung cancer patients would qualify for advance screening based on eligibility guidelines
medical.summary: A new data analysis of Southern California lung cancer patients has found that only 13% would have met eligibility criteria for advance screening despite expanded eligibility guidelines issued in 2021. Female, Asian and Hispanic patients were significantly less likely to be eligible for lung cancer screening. The findings from the new study in the Journal of the American College of Radiology highlight the limited reach of existing eligibility criteria, especially in underrepresented populations.

medical.title: Cholesterol plaques in the neck and legs signal increased cardiac risk
medical.summary: Atherosclerosis does not respect anatomical territories. Once cholesterol plaques appear in the arteries, they tend to spread throughout different regions of the arterial system. A new analysis from the PESA (Progression of Early Subclinical Atherosclerosis) study, led by researchers at the Centro Nacional de Investigaciones Cardiovasculares Carlos III (CNIC) under the direction of principal investigator Dr. Valentín Fuster, shows that the presence and extent of plaques in the neck (carotid) and leg (femoral) arteries are closely associated with the presence, severity and burden of atherosclerosis in the coronary arteries.

medical.title: Whole-genome sequencing study reveals how antibiotic-resistant bacteria may spread through rural communities in Malawi
medical.summary: A new study led by researchers at Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine (LSTM) has shed light on how antibiotic-resistant bacteria spread within rural communities in Malawi.

medical.title: Older drivers are not making the roads unsafe, research shows
medical.summary: Changes to medical fitness testing for South Australian drivers have not made the roads less safe, a new report from Adelaide University has found.

medical.title: Can AI expedite medical imaging? Yes—if we can trust the picture
medical.summary: When it comes to medical imaging, everyone wants better technology faster—but no one wants to cut corners on health and safety. Enter a new statistical tool that determines whether AI-generated data could accurately stand in for patient data in clinical trials.

medical.title: Fatigue can persist even after a good recovery from stroke
medical.summary: In a study of life after stroke, one survivor described doing less during the day if they planned to see friends that evening. When you're living with fatigue, even an ordinary day can take that kind of planning. Going out may mean deciding what else can wait until tomorrow.

medical.title: Inflammatory sensor offers a target for new therapies in patients with brain injuries
medical.summary: A traumatic brain injury can have a lasting impact on a person's life. Beyond the immediate damage caused by the impact, subsequent processes can further impair brain function. These include inflammatory responses, which normally support defense and repair but can contribute to additional damage when strongly or persistently activated.

medical.title: One in four students turn to AI for mental health support
medical.summary: New research finds students are using AI for emotional support, including when distressed and as a personal therapist or coach.

science.title: Ultracold atoms reveal first direct view of bound-pair motion in a fracton system
science.summary: Particles can generally move between neighboring sites in a crystal, a solid in which atoms are arranged in a regular, repeating pattern, or an optical lattice, an arrangement of laser-based traps that confines atoms. A strong potential gradient (i.e., a steep change in potential energy across a crystal or lattice) makes this ordinary particle hopping difficult and energetically costly.

science.title: 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals an ingenious waterproofing trick
science.summary: A 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck has revealed sophisticated waterproofing techniques involving pine tar and beeswax. Microscopic pollen grains trapped in the ancient coatings are now helping scientists reconstruct where the vessel may have traveled and undergone repairs more than two millennia ago.

science.title: Ancient rocks from the Moon’s far side rewrite the Solar System’s violent past
science.summary: Scientists studying ancient rocks from the Moon’s far side have uncovered surprising evidence that challenges decades of thinking about the Solar System’s violent past. Instead of a single catastrophic bombardment, asteroid impacts appear to have declined gradually over billions of years, revealing new clues about Earth's early evolution and the origins of life.

science.title: China unveils new space mission crew, with a Pakistani astronaut set to board its space station
science.summary: China on Tuesday unveiled the crew for its Shenzhou 24 spacecraft ahead of this week's launch, with a Pakistani set to become the first foreign astronaut to board its space station.

science.title: New quasar record tightens constraints on black hole formation scenarios
science.summary: A team of astronomers led by Julien Wolf, a postdoctoral researcher at the Max Planck Institute for Astronomy (MPIA) in Heidelberg, Germany (now at the European Southern Observatory in Garching bei München, Germany), discovered the most distant quasar to date. First identified in the Euclid Wide Survey (EWS), the object was confirmed to be a quasar by subsequent observations with some of the most powerful telescopes on the ground and in space.

science.title: Workplace absenteeism: Why temporary disability is a right, not an expense
science.summary: Temporary disability is a cornerstone of the public Social Security system. It is a right for all workers who fall ill and a social security benefit designed primarily to protect those who are sick, enabling them to receive medical treatment and recover or improve their condition while ensuring they have sufficient income during periods in which they are unable to work.

science.title: New light-conversion tool could help speed up quantum computing

science.title: Earth’s ancient oceans may have fooled scientists about its oxygen history
science.summary: Earth’s journey from an oxygen-starved world to a planet capable of supporting complex life may have unfolded very differently than scientists once believed. A new analysis suggests that oxygen accumulated in the atmosphere in three major stages, with the oceans taking millions or even hundreds of millions of years to catch up.

science.title: Earth's core may be leaking a 4.5-billion-year-old secret
science.summary: Scientists have discovered an unusual carbon signature in Hawaiian volcanic rocks that suggests some of Earth's carbon originated in ancient meteorites and later escaped from deep within the planet's core. The discovery raises an astonishing possibility: Carbon essential to life may have traveled from space to Earth's depths before emerging through volcanoes billions of years later.

environment.title: The mystery of how hair knows where to grow may finally be solved
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered that the intricate patterns of hair follicles on mammals may arise from a remarkably simple process involving cells following chemical signals. The findings challenge a long-standing theory and reveal how nature can create complex biological patterns without a detailed blueprint.

environment.title: NASA reveals Earth's ozone hole has grown to a size not seen in a decade
environment.summary: The Antarctic ozone hole expanded to its seventh-largest size on record in 2026, driven by unusual weather conditions that pushed it close to its historic maximum. Scientists say international restrictions on ozone-destroying chemicals prevented even greater damage, and Earth's protective ozone layer is still recovering.

environment.title: Scientists uncover a 192-year-old mystery hidden in a mangled silver coin
environment.summary: A bizarrely deformed 1834 British silver coin found at a car boot sale may preserve evidence of a rare minting accident nearly 200 years ago. Advanced 3D scans and microscopic analysis revealed unusual metal distortions suggesting the coin was crushed under extreme pressure, potentially during its original production.

environment.title: Where are all the males? Ancient human fossils reveal a startling mystery
environment.summary: A remarkable discovery in a South African cave suggests that an extinct human relative may have created an all-female burial site more than 240,000 years ago. Scientists analyzed ancient proteins preserved in Homo naledi teeth and found no male-specific markers among at least 20 individuals, potentially solving a mystery that has puzzled researchers for over a decade.

environment.title: Scientists just found dinosaur blood that survived 115 million years
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered chemically confirmed traces of ancient blood inside 115-million-year-old dinosaur bones, challenging assumptions about how long biological molecules can survive. The extraordinary preservation could unlock new clues about dinosaur physiology and even help scientists search for ancient life elsewhere in the universe.

environment.title: The Great Barrier Reef's most notorious coral killer may actually be helping it
environment.summary: Crown-of-thorns starfish are notorious for devouring coral reefs, but surprising new research reveals these spiny predators may actually help reefs thrive when their populations are kept in check. Scientists studying Australia's Great Barrier Reef discovered that nearly 75% of observed starfish feeding events left behind living coral tissue, rather than destroying entire colonies. By feeding on fast-growing, dominant corals, the starfish create opportunities for slower-growing species to survive, potentially increasing coral biodiversity.

environment.title: Ancient ape fossil in Egypt could rewrite the story of human origins
environment.summary: A 17- to 18-million-year-old ape fossil discovered in Egypt is challenging long-held beliefs about where the ancestors of humans and other modern apes first evolved. Scientists now suspect that North Africa and the Middle East, rather than East Africa, may have been the cradle of modern ape evolution.

environment.title: Scientists discover the hidden “muscles” trees use to straighten themselves
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered that trees can sense their own shape and straighten their trunks using specialized wood that acts like opposing muscles. This remarkable ability helps trees maintain their posture and could lead to stronger forests, better timber, and more resilient crops.

mix_items.title: Music before and during coronary angiography linked to lower blood pressure
mix_items.summary: Music therapy before and during an often stressful procedure to visualize blood flow to coronary arteries (coronary angiography) is associated with lower systolic blood pressure—the higher number in a reading—according to the results of a comparative clinical trial published online in the journal Heart.

mix_items.title: From primal instinct to persistent preoccupation: Measuring 'food noise'
mix_items.summary: How people think about food continues to evolve. For early hunter-gatherers, food meant survival. Thoughts about food focused mainly on where to find it. As people learned to farm, thoughts about food shifted from something hunted or caught to something cultivated.

mix_items.title: Parents strongly accept intestinal ultrasound for pediatric IBD monitoring
mix_items.summary: Parents of children with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) report strong acceptance of intestinal ultrasound (IUS) for disease monitoring, according to a study published online Nov. 17 in JPGN Reports.

mix_items.title: Could blowing your nose make cold symptoms worse?
mix_items.summary: Few things are more frustrating than dealing with a runny nose when you're sick. No matter how many times you blow your nose, a few minutes later it's full of snot again and the sniffles are back.

mix_items.title: Many languages, one common neural code
'I'm amazed every day': Woman marks one year with a pig kidney
mix_items.summary: A New Hampshire woman has now lived for one year with a kidney from a gene-edited pig, the longest any patient is known to have done so.

mix_items.title: Significant decrease in Black-white mortality gap during past 30 years
mix_items.summary: A major health gap in America is shrinking. A new study by researchers at the American Cancer Society (ACS) shows the historic divide in death rates between Black and white men and women in the United States narrowed dramatically between 1993 and 2023. Excess mortality among Black adults plummeted by 56% for men and 68% for women.

mix_items.title: AI can predict antidepressant response, but does not understand all patients equally
mix_items.summary: George Mason University researchers have revealed just how much health literacy can influence AI's ability to understand patients. In a new study involving simulated patients, an AI antidepressant decision aid correctly identified medical information 82% of the time when patients used precise medical language, but less than half the time when they described their health in vaguer or more informal terms.

mix_items.title: When antidepressants don't help, could ketamine be an option?
mix_items.summary: Once known mainly as a surgical anesthetic, ketamine is now an option for people whose depression hasn't eased with standard medications and therapy.

mix_items.title: How the brain's visual system shapes lasting fear memories
mix_items.summary: Researchers at McGovern Medical School at UTHealth Houston have discovered how the brain's visual system plays an active role in transforming threatening experiences into lasting fear memories and how noninvasive brain stimulation can interrupt this process.

mix_items.title: Not just a phase: Measuring the long-term toll of high school substance use
mix_items.summary: High schoolers who smoke cigarettes, use cannabis or take other drugs face a higher risk of dying earlier in adulthood, according to a five-decade University of Michigan study.

mix_items.title: New Year's resolutions: Starting small today could work better than waiting until January
mix_items.summary: Every year, millions of people promise to start the new year by losing weight, eating better and exercising more. January feels like a natural moment for a fresh start. But big resolutions create a lot of pressure and are hard to keep up.

mix_items.title: Lack of data hinders genetic screening for heart failure in the Brazilian population
mix_items.summary: The low representation of Brazilians in global genomic databases compromises the accuracy of tests used to investigate the causes of heart failure. This is according to a study by the University of São Paulo (USP), which revealed an additional limitation of these tests: interpreting results is significantly more difficult when analyzing DNA segments of African or Indigenous ancestry.

mix_items.title: How sensory neurons help the brain pursue its goals
mix_items.summary: A new Yale study offers insight into a fundamental question in neuroscience: How does the nervous system transform sensory information into signals that help us achieve our goals?

mix_items.title: One in 12 children with Lyme disease show signs of Powassan virus co-infection
mix_items.summary: The prevalence of Powassan virus infection in U.S. children with suspected Lyme disease is higher than previously thought, according to a new study published in Clinical Infectious Diseases.

mix_items.title: Only 13% of lung cancer patients would qualify for advance screening based on eligibility guidelines
mix_items.summary: A new data analysis of Southern California lung cancer patients has found that only 13% would have met eligibility criteria for advance screening despite expanded eligibility guidelines issued in 2021. Female, Asian and Hispanic patients were significantly less likely to be eligible for lung cancer screening. The findings from the new study in the Journal of the American College of Radiology highlight the limited reach of existing eligibility criteria, especially in underrepresented populations.

mix_items.title: Cholesterol plaques in the neck and legs signal increased cardiac risk
mix_items.summary: Atherosclerosis does not respect anatomical territories. Once cholesterol plaques appear in the arteries, they tend to spread throughout different regions of the arterial system. A new analysis from the PESA (Progression of Early Subclinical Atherosclerosis) study, led by researchers at the Centro Nacional de Investigaciones Cardiovasculares Carlos III (CNIC) under the direction of principal investigator Dr. Valentín Fuster, shows that the presence and extent of plaques in the neck (carotid) and leg (femoral) arteries are closely associated with the presence, severity and burden of atherosclerosis in the coronary arteries.

mix_items.title: Whole-genome sequencing study reveals how antibiotic-resistant bacteria may spread through rural communities in Malawi
mix_items.summary: A new study led by researchers at Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine (LSTM) has shed light on how antibiotic-resistant bacteria spread within rural communities in Malawi.

mix_items.title: Older drivers are not making the roads unsafe, research shows
mix_items.summary: Changes to medical fitness testing for South Australian drivers have not made the roads less safe, a new report from Adelaide University has found.

mix_items.title: Can AI expedite medical imaging? Yes—if we can trust the picture
mix_items.summary: When it comes to medical imaging, everyone wants better technology faster—but no one wants to cut corners on health and safety. Enter a new statistical tool that determines whether AI-generated data could accurately stand in for patient data in clinical trials.

mix_items.title: Fatigue can persist even after a good recovery from stroke
mix_items.summary: In a study of life after stroke, one survivor described doing less during the day if they planned to see friends that evening. When you're living with fatigue, even an ordinary day can take that kind of planning. Going out may mean deciding what else can wait until tomorrow.

mix_items.title: Inflammatory sensor offers a target for new therapies in patients with brain injuries
mix_items.summary: A traumatic brain injury can have a lasting impact on a person's life. Beyond the immediate damage caused by the impact, subsequent processes can further impair brain function. These include inflammatory responses, which normally support defense and repair but can contribute to additional damage when strongly or persistently activated.

mix_items.title: One in four students turn to AI for mental health support
mix_items.summary: New research finds students are using AI for emotional support, including when distressed and as a personal therapist or coach.

mix_items.title: Earth's core may be leaking a 4.5-billion-year-old secret
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered an unusual carbon signature in Hawaiian volcanic rocks that suggests some of Earth's carbon originated in ancient meteorites and later escaped from deep within the planet's core. The discovery raises an astonishing possibility: Carbon essential to life may have traveled from space to Earth's depths before emerging through volcanoes billions of years later.

mix_items.title: The mystery of how hair knows where to grow may finally be solved
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that the intricate patterns of hair follicles on mammals may arise from a remarkably simple process involving cells following chemical signals. The findings challenge a long-standing theory and reveal how nature can create complex biological patterns without a detailed blueprint.

mix_items.title: NASA reveals Earth's ozone hole has grown to a size not seen in a decade
mix_items.summary: The Antarctic ozone hole expanded to its seventh-largest size on record in 2026, driven by unusual weather conditions that pushed it close to its historic maximum. Scientists say international restrictions on ozone-destroying chemicals prevented even greater damage, and Earth's protective ozone layer is still recovering.

mix_items.title: Scientists uncover a 192-year-old mystery hidden in a mangled silver coin
mix_items.summary: A bizarrely deformed 1834 British silver coin found at a car boot sale may preserve evidence of a rare minting accident nearly 200 years ago. Advanced 3D scans and microscopic analysis revealed unusual metal distortions suggesting the coin was crushed under extreme pressure, potentially during its original production.

mix_items.title: Where are all the males? Ancient human fossils reveal a startling mystery
mix_items.summary: A remarkable discovery in a South African cave suggests that an extinct human relative may have created an all-female burial site more than 240,000 years ago. Scientists analyzed ancient proteins preserved in Homo naledi teeth and found no male-specific markers among at least 20 individuals, potentially solving a mystery that has puzzled researchers for over a decade.

mix_items.title: Scientists just found dinosaur blood that survived 115 million years
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered chemically confirmed traces of ancient blood inside 115-million-year-old dinosaur bones, challenging assumptions about how long biological molecules can survive. The extraordinary preservation could unlock new clues about dinosaur physiology and even help scientists search for ancient life elsewhere in the universe.

mix_items.title: The Great Barrier Reef's most notorious coral killer may actually be helping it
mix_items.summary: Crown-of-thorns starfish are notorious for devouring coral reefs, but surprising new research reveals these spiny predators may actually help reefs thrive when their populations are kept in check. Scientists studying Australia's Great Barrier Reef discovered that nearly 75% of observed starfish feeding events left behind living coral tissue, rather than destroying entire colonies. By feeding on fast-growing, dominant corals, the starfish create opportunities for slower-growing species to survive, potentially increasing coral biodiversity.

mix_items.title: Ancient ape fossil in Egypt could rewrite the story of human origins
mix_items.summary: A 17- to 18-million-year-old ape fossil discovered in Egypt is challenging long-held beliefs about where the ancestors of humans and other modern apes first evolved. Scientists now suspect that North Africa and the Middle East, rather than East Africa, may have been the cradle of modern ape evolution.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover the hidden “muscles” trees use to straighten themselves
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that trees can sense their own shape and straighten their trunks using specialized wood that acts like opposing muscles. This remarkable ability helps trees maintain their posture and could lead to stronger forests, better timber, and more resilient crops.
